title: Modern Times
synopsis: A factory, a paddy wagon, a department store, and a tramp who keeps walking up the road toward the next horizon.

nodes.text: Two salesmen wheel it in and the boss picks you because you are nearest the door. They strap a bib on. There is a rotating corn cob, a soup plate on a tilt, and an automatic mouth-wiper. The soup plate is what worries you. The mouth-wiper is what should worry you.

choices.consequence: You sit down in the chair yourself, hands folded, ready to be efficient. Nobody in the history of this factory has volunteered for anything.

You get behind a crate and are found in four seconds, because you are the only man on the floor holding his breath. You choose to hide. By Conveyor Belt, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Two bolts on every plate, and the plates keep coming. Scratch your nose and you are three plates behind; sneeze and you are nine. The foreman watches from a window and the belt goes faster after lunch, and your arms keep tightening things in the air long after the plates run out.

choices.consequence: You match the belt for two hours and win, and your hands go on winning by themselves right through the lunch break. You choose to keep up. By Gears, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You let four plates go past unbolted. Somewhere down the line a machine is now being assembled with holes in it. You slow down. It gets you to Gears, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You go after a loose spanner and the belt takes your sleeve, then the rest of you, and you travel through the machine lying down. Cogs pass you along like a parcel. In there, at the center of everything, you tighten two bolts nobody has reached in years. Then the wheel reverses.

choices.consequence: You raise one hand to the crew as you disappear into the works, because a man should acknowledge people when passing. You commit to wave on the way. The road to Hospital is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You go in shouting and come out still shouting, and find the shout has been running some while on its own. You choose to scream. By Hospital, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: A doctor holds your jaw, says ah, and delivers a lecture on the nervous system while your right hand tightens two invisible bolts on his lapel. He calls it a full recovery. He also advises you to avoid excitement. Then he signs you out onto a street with a strike on it.

choices.consequence: You thank him, shake his hand, and give it a quarter turn on the way past. He decides not to mention that. You commit to smile and leave. The road to Flag is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You explain about the belt, in gestures, at length. He writes REST on a card and hands you a leaflet about fresh air. You commit to argue. The road to Flag is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: A lumber truck drops a red warning flag in the road. You pick it up and wave it after the driver, and the driver does not look back, and four thousand marching people come around the corner behind you in perfect step. You are now at the front of something. Mounted police arrive shortly.

choices.consequence: You keep waving politely at a truck that is three blocks away by now, leading a movement nobody has briefed you on. You choose to wave it gently. By Cell, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You let the flag fall the instant you understand. Four officers have already decided which one of you is the organizer. You drop it. It gets you to Cell, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Your cellmate keeps his powder in the salt shaker and watches you steadily while you reach for it. You put an entire snowfall on your beans. Twenty minutes later the walls are friendly, the bars are a suggestion, and a jailbreak is starting in the corridor without you.

choices.consequence: You season generously, on the theory that a condiment is a condiment, and spend the afternoon convinced you are extremely tall. You commit to salt your soup. The road to Pardon is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You push the shaker back and eat your beans plain, which is the only correct decision you make all week. You refuse. It gets you to Pardon, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The warden shakes your hand for stopping a breakout you have no memory of stopping. There is a letter. It says you are honest and industrious, and it is signed by a man with a very good pen. He is handing you your freedom. You would rather have the cell, and you cannot say so.

choices.consequence: You fold the letter into your inside pocket, where it will stay dry through three jobs and outlast every one of them. You commit to take it. The road to Gamin is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You mime that you are comfortable here and the food agrees with you. The warden laughs and holds the gate open. You choose to stay in the cell. By Gamin, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: She comes off the dock at a dead run with bananas under both arms and hands one to a small child without slowing down. Bare feet, cut rope for a belt, a grin like a struck match. Two officers are forty yards back and losing ground. You are standing directly in her path.

choices.consequence: You step sideways into the officers' route and apologize at enormous length while she goes past you and around the corner. You commit to help her. The road to Pawnbroker is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You mind your own business for a full three seconds, then put out a foot, which is not minding your own business. You walk on. It gets you to Pawnbroker, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: She puts a lady's watch on the counter with the chain coiled beside it and does not say whose it was. The broker turns it over, breathes on the case, and names a figure. She takes the figure without arguing, which tells you she has done this before, with other things, that are already gone.

choices.consequence: You nod her toward the counter because two people need supper tonight, and you carry the guilt out into the street on her behalf. You choose to pawn it. By Shipyard, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You put your hand flat over the watch and shake your head, having no money, no plan, and one very firm opinion. You commit to refuse. The road to Shipyard is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The foreman points at a timber wedge and walks off. You go in under the hull, find the wedge, and pull. The ship moves. The ship keeps moving. Eighty tons of unfinished vessel enters the harbor stern-first with no keel in it and goes down in perfect silence while you hold the wedge.

choices.consequence: You take off your hat to the harbor. Somewhere behind you a foreman is making a sound no man should make. You choose to apologize. By Department Store, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You set the wedge down neatly, as though tidiness helps, and leave the yard at a brisk walk without turning around. You commit to run. The road to Department Store is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: The store at night is six floors of everything nobody you know can afford. She tries on a fur coat and falls asleep in the bed department. You lace on skates and take her to the toy floor, where the railing is off for repairs and there is a four-story drop where the floor stops.

choices.consequence: You tie a scarf over your eyes to impress her and glide backwards to within four inches of the edge, twice. You choose to skate blindfolded. By Thieves, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You keep both eyes open and stay near the counters, and she watches you being sensible and looks faintly let down. You choose to skate carefully. By Thieves, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Three men with a crowbar in the grocery department, and the biggest one lowers it and says your name. You worked the same belt. They are not here for the till; they are here because they are hungry, and one of them has already got a tin open using his hands.

choices.consequence: You fetch glasses and they fetch the rum, and by two in the morning the four of you are singing in bedding. You choose to share the food. By Shack on the Lake, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You get halfway to the telephone, look back at a man eating cold beans off a crowbar, and stop where you stand. You call the police. It gets you to Shack on the Lake, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: She has found a place. The door comes off in your hand on arrival. The ceiling drops a plank on your head when you sit down, the far wall opens onto the lake when you lean on it, and the front step throws you into the water when you use it. She calls it paradise. She means it.

choices.consequence: You carry her over a threshold that detaches on contact, and you both stay anyway, and you mend the step on Sunday. You commit to move in. The road to Newspaper Help-Wanted is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You suggest looking further along the shore. She is already hanging a curtain made out of a flour sack, so that settles that. You commit to find better. The road to Newspaper Help-Wanted is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: She holds the paper up before you are properly awake: the plant is opening. Eight hundred men are at the gates when you get there, pressed against the iron, quiet in a way crowds are not usually quiet. The gates go back. You are carried through them without your feet touching anything.

choices.consequence: You take the job at the mechanic's bench and are, for one entire morning, a man with employment and a lunch pail. You commit to apply. The road to Strike is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You turn over for ten more minutes and she hauls you upright by the ankles, and you are at the gates by seven. You choose to sleep in. By Strike, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Your foot happens to be resting on a loose brick when the picket line comes past and a police wagon slows. The brick shifts. You catch it on your instep, flick it up, and there you are, holding a brick, in the street, during a strike, with an officer already writing.

choices.consequence: You wave, because waving has served you so well historically, and this time you are waving with a brick in your hand. You wave again. It gets you to Cafe Job, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You set the brick down with enormous care, as though it might be evidence, which it is, and then you go. You choose to run. By Cafe Job, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: She has talked her way into a singing job and talked you into an apron. The kitchen door swings both ways and the dance floor lies between you and table four. You are carrying a roast duck at head height through a foxtrot. The duck leaves the tray during the second chorus.

choices.consequence: You go in among the dancers with the tray held overhead and come out the far side having lost only the garnish. You choose to take the floor. By Performer, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You untie the apron twice and put it back on twice, because she is up on that stage and you are not leaving her here. You choose to quit. By Performer, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The lyrics are written on your cuffs. You flick your wrists on the way to the microphone and both cuffs sail into the orchestra pit. The band starts. You do not know one word of this song. Two hundred people are watching and the tenor sax has already begun the introduction.

choices.consequence: You act the whole thing out with your hips and your eyebrows, and a room full of strangers understands every verse. You mime the song. It gets you to Authorities at the Door, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You invent a language on the spot, commit to it completely, and take an encore in a tongue that does not exist. You commit to sing nonsense. The road to Authorities at the Door is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Two officers come into the cafe with a folder and her name inside it. She is a minor with no address and a father in a file. The manager points at the stage. She is halfway through the second number, and she sees them over the top of the room, and keeps singing.

choices.consequence: You take her hand at the kitchen door and go out through the alley in an apron and skates, and keep going. You run with her. It gets you to Truck on the Highway, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You put yourself between her and the folder and make a reasonable case in mime, and reasonable has never once worked for you. You submit. It gets you to Truck on the Highway, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Dawn on the county road, and a flatbed slows without being asked. The driver jerks his thumb at the back and wants neither a name nor a reason. You ride out of the city on a stack of empty crates with her shoes in your lap, the two of you facing backwards.

choices.consequence: You run alongside, throw her up first, and get one leg over the tailgate with the last thing you had left. You choose to catch it. By Open Country, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You wave the truck on and take the road on foot, because it is a good morning and you would rather see it slowly. You choose to walk. By Open Country, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: No fence, no whistle, no gate. The road runs out between two fields, turns behind a hill, and does not explain itself. She has stopped walking. She is sitting on the verge with her arms around her knees, and she has run out of whatever has been carrying her since the dock.

choices.consequence: You hum four bars of the song with no words and get it wrong on purpose until she tells you to stop. You sing to her. It gets you to Smile, She Cries, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You sit down beside her on the verge and say nothing whatsoever for a while, which is your best language anyway. You choose to just walk. By Smile, She Cries, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: The dust on the verge is warm and the light is coming up behind the hill. What is the use, she says. You crouch in front of her and put one finger at each corner of her mouth and push them upward, and hold them there, and wait. Then you take your hands away to see whether anything stays.

choices.consequence: It holds a second on its own, then goes crooked, then turns real, and she gets up and fixes her hair. You commit to make her smile. The road to Up the Road is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You skip the trick entirely and lift her hand off her knee, and she lets you, and neither of you mentions it. You hold her hand. It gets you to Waiter on Wheels, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

There is a way this morning goes that has nothing to do with the road, and it begins with a whistle at six. You commit to take the third path. The road to The Wheel Goes On is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: You brush the dust off her and off yourself, and you both set your hats, and you go. The road climbs, bends, and carries the two of you out of sight of anything that keeps a payroll. Nobody has offered you a job or a house or a reason. There is only the road, a woman who can outrun a policeman, and a morning that has not been spent yet.

The manager puts you on nights permanently and gives her a dressing room with a mirror and a chair that is hers. You learn nine words of the song and invent the rest, and the regulars come specifically for the part where you get it wrong. She keeps the tips in a coffee tin behind the bar. On Sundays you skate the empty floor with the chairs stacked and the lights down.

At dawn you are at the gates before the gates are open, first in a line of eight hundred, holding a lunch pail she packed. The whistle goes at six. You pull on the coveralls, take your place at the belt, and the plates start coming, two bolts each, forever. Somewhere in the third hour you catch yourself whistling. You would not admit that to anybody, including her.
